teaser: An angel brings the best news in Christianity. So why is Mary pulling away from him?
review_notes:
The image shows only the central Annunciation panel; the side saints named in the title (Ansanus and Margaret) are cropped out. The lesson says so.
Olive branch instead of lily explained by Siena's rivalry with Florence: a traditional explanation, presented as such.
The identity of the female saint (Margaret, Maxima or Giulitta) is debated; lesson keeps the catalog title.
Empty central roundel 'probably held God the Father': usual hypothesis.
Raised (relief) lettering of the angel's greeting; Petrarch's sonnets on Simone's portrait of Laura; frame remade in the 19th century; moved to the Uffizi in 1799.

lesson.text: Something does not add up here. An angel has just landed with the happiest message a woman in this story could receive: she will be the mother of God. And the woman twists away from him, pulls her cloak to her throat and frowns. Simone Martini painted good news that is received like a threat.

The scene is the Annunciation, told in the Gospel of Luke. The angel Gabriel appears to Mary and greets her. Luke adds one small line that most painters skipped: she was troubled by his words. Simone built his whole picture on that one line.

lesson.title: A sentence crossing the gold
lesson.text: Follow the message from the one who speaks it to the one who hears it.

spots.title: The speaker
spots.text: Gabriel's lips are parted. He wears a crown of olive leaves and his eyes are fixed straight ahead. He is in the middle of speaking.

spots.title: The words
spots.text: Letters run through the air from his mouth toward her ear: Ave gratia plena Dominus tecum. “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” Speech, made visible.

spots.title: The listener
spots.text: Mary's head tilts away, her mouth turns down, her eyes narrow. One hand closes the cloak at her neck, the way you would against a cold draft.

spots.title: The interrupted page
spots.text: Her thumb is still tucked inside the red book to keep her place. She was reading a second ago. The visit has caught her mid-sentence.

lesson.text: So the picture is a conversation, and you just read it left to right like a line of text. Around 1333 that was a bold idea. Holy figures were usually shown calm and frontal, outside of time. Here there is a before, a now, and a reply that has not come yet.

The angel's greeting is not simply painted on. The letters stand up from the surface in low relief, built in plaster and then gilded, so that candlelight in the cathedral would catch them and make the sentence flicker.

The background is real gold, beaten into leaves thinner than paper and laid over a red clay base. No room, no sky, no shadow. For a medieval viewer this glow was not a place but a signal: what happens here happens in the presence of heaven.
Simone Martini gave a sacred scene the timing of a human one: a word spoken, a body that flinches, an answer still to come.

Simone came from Siena, a rich Tuscan city of bankers and wool merchants, proud of its cathedral and devoted to the Virgin. He signed this altarpiece together with his brother-in-law Lippo Memmi. It was made for the cathedral, for an altar dedicated to Saint Ansanus, one of the city's protectors.
The signature runs along the bottom of the frame and names both painters with the date 1333. It does not say who painted what, and specialists have been arguing over the division of hands ever since.

The title promises two saints, Ansanus and Margaret. They stand on separate panels to the left and right, and this image stops just before them: you only get the central scene, between two twisted columns. One more heavenly visitor is in view, though, and it is easy to miss.
A dove is flying somewhere in this picture. Can you tap it?

spots.title: The Holy Spirit
spots.text: The dove dives head first out of a ring of winged angel heads, straight down the central axis. In Christian painting it stands for the Holy Spirit, by whom Mary conceives.

lesson.text: Directly below the dove stands a vase of white lilies, the usual sign of Mary's purity. In most Annunciations the angel carries the lily himself. Simone's Gabriel holds an olive branch, the emblem of peace, and the lilies are left to stand on the floor.
A long-standing explanation for that swap is politics. The lily was the badge of Florence, Siena's great enemy, and a Sienese angel could hardly be seen waving it in Siena's own cathedral.

Now forget the story and watch the outlines. Simone was trained in the world of Gothic art, the style of pointed arches and slim, swaying figures that came from northern Europe. His strength is the edge of things: a contour that bends like handwriting.
Three shapes carry the whole drama. Trace them one by one.

lines.label: The arrival
lines.text: The plaid cloak still streams out behind the angel and the wings are still raised. Everything on this side pushes to the right. He has only just touched the ground.

lines.label: The recoil
lines.text: Mary's dark blue body is one long S that leans back into the corner of her throne. The curve does the acting: it is the shape of someone drawing in.

lines.label: The gap
lines.text: Between them, an empty strip of gold with only the dove and the lilies on it. Nothing crosses it but the sentence. Simone leaves the distance open on purpose.

lesson.text: Notice how flat Mary's robe is: a single blue silhouette with a thin gold hem wandering around it. Simone is not trying to convince you of weight or depth. He wants the outline to carry the feeling, and it does.

The gilded arches and pinnacles around the scene are not his. The original frame was lost, and this one was made in the 19th century in Gothic style. The round opening at the very top is empty today. It probably once held an image of God the Father, sending the dove on its way.

spots.title: The wings
spots.text: Feathers patterned like a peacock's, with rows of eyes along the edge, still lifted from the flight.

spots.title: Olive branch
spots.text: Gabriel's left hand holds the olive branch upright. His right hand, just beside it, is raised with a pointing finger: the gesture of someone speaking.

spots.title: The lilies
spots.text: White lilies in a gilded two-handled vase, placed exactly between the two figures. They stand for Mary's purity.

spots.title: A prophet
spots.text: In the small circles above, bearded prophets hold scrolls. They are the Old Testament voices said to have foretold this moment.

spots.title: The empty circle
spots.text: A blank gold disc where a painted figure, probably God the Father, has gone missing.

spots.title: The throne
spots.text: Mary's seat is inlaid with small geometric patterns, like the costly marble and wood furniture of Simone's own day.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Along the base of the frame runs the Latin inscription naming Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi of Siena and the year 1333.

lesson.text: A few years later Simone left Italy for Avignon, in the south of France, where the popes then held court. He befriended the poet Petrarch, who wrote two sonnets about a portrait Simone made of his beloved Laura. He died there in 1344. His swaying line traveled through the courts of Europe for the next hundred years.

The altarpiece stayed in Siena Cathedral for centuries before it was moved to Florence in 1799, into the Uffizi. So the angel who refused the Florentine lily ended up living in Florence after all. And Mary, seven hundred years on, has still not given her answer.

quiz.question: How does Mary react to the angel in this painting?
options: She shrinks back and closes her cloak
She keeps reading and ignores him
quiz.explanation: Simone shows her troubled, twisting away with one hand at her throat.

quiz.question: What is special about the angel's words in the picture?
options: They cross the gold in raised, gilded letters
They are written in a book he holds
They were added in the 19th century
quiz.explanation: The greeting runs from his mouth toward Mary in low relief.

quiz.question: What does Gabriel hold instead of the usual lily?
quiz.explanation: He carries an olive branch, while the lilies stand in a vase on the floor.

quiz.question: For which building was the altarpiece made?
quiz.explanation: It was painted for an altar of Saint Ansanus in Siena Cathedral.

quiz.question: Who signed the work together with Simone Martini?
quiz.explanation: His brother-in-law Lippo Memmi is named beside him on the frame.

quiz.question: What does the dove among the angels stand for?
quiz.explanation: In Christian painting the dove represents the Holy Spirit.

facts.text: The gilded Gothic frame around the scene is the original one from 1333.
facts.explanation: The original frame was lost and this one was made in the 19th century.

facts.text: The background is made of real gold leaf.
facts.explanation: Thin leaves of beaten gold were laid over a red clay base.

facts.text: Simone Martini spent his last years in Avignon, where he knew the poet Petrarch.
facts.explanation: He moved to the papal court in Avignon and died there in 1344.
